states.activities:
​​​​No data will flow to NHS England o for the purposes of this Data Sharing Agreement (DSA).

​​​​NHS England will grant access to the Data via the Secure Data Environment (SDE).  The SDE is a secure data and research analysis platform. It allows approved researchers with approved projects access to pseudonymised data and industry-leading analytics tools.     

​​NHS England will provide access to the relevant records from the NDRS Cancer Consolidated Dataset to University of Cambridge via NHS England Secure Data Environment (SDE). The Data will contain no direct identifying data items. The Data will be pseudonymised and individuals cannot be reidentified.   

​SDE users can request exportation of aggregated analysis results (suppressed and summarised according to the NHSE SDE Disclosure Control rules) subject to review and approval by the NHS England SDE Output Checking team. The SDE Output Checking team will ensure that no output contains information which could be used either on its own or in conjunction with other data to breach an individual's privacy.     

​Users must identify themselves via a multi-factor authentication mechanism and are only able to access the datasets detailed within this DSA. The access and use of the system is fully auditable, and all users must comply with the use of the Data as specified in this DSA.   

​  ​​Users are only authorised to access the Data specified in this DSA and can utilise a variety of analytical tools available within the SDE platform. Users are not permitted to export record-level data from the SDE.    

The Data will not be transferred to any other location.​ 

​​The Data will be stored on servers at NHSE Secure Data Environment​.

The Data will be accessed by authorised personnel via remote access.    ​

​​The Controller(s) must confirm and provide evidence upon audit by NHS England that access via any remote device complies with the data security obligations within this DSA and the Data Sharing Framework Contract.  
​​ 
​​For remote access:  

​​•	Remote access will only be from secure locations situated within the territory of use (as further restricted elsewhere within the DSA if so done) stated within this DSA.  

​​•	Access controls granting users the minimum level of access required are in place.  

​​•	Remote access is only via secure connections (e.g., VPNs or secure protocols) to protect data.  

​​•	Multifactor authentication (MFA) is required for remote access.  

​​•	Device security, including up-to-date software and operating systems, antivirus software, and enabled firewalls are utilised for the remote access.  

​​•	All remote access is undertaken within the scope of the organisation’s DSPT (or other security arrangements as per this DSA) and complies with the organisation’s remote access policy.  

​​  ​​The above applies in addition to any condition set out elsewhere within the DSA (e.g. who may carry out processing, and for what purpose).​  

​The Data will not be linked with any other data outside of this DSA.​

states.expected_benefits:
​​The findings of this research study are expected to contribute to evidence-based decision-making for policymakers, local decision-makers such as doctors, and patients to inform best practice to improve the care, treatment and experience of health care users relevant to the subject matter of the study.  

​​The use of the data could:  

​​Help the system to better understand the health and care needs of populations, particularly in relation to cancer progression, diagnostic delay, and outcomes across different cancers and population groups. 

​Lead to improved understanding of how diagnostic delay affects stage at diagnosis and mortality, supporting earlier detection and better patient outcomes. 

​Inform the design and refinement of diagnostic pathways and screening strategies, including evaluation of more tailored and equitable approaches to breast cancer screening. 

​Advance understanding of inequalities in cancer outcomes, including variation by ethnicity and socioeconomic status, supporting more equitable service delivery 

​Inform planning of health services and programmes by providing evidence on cancer-specific diagnostic timelines and service needs. 

​Support decisions on how to prioritise resources and manage the economic burden of delayed diagnosis, through analysis of cost and outcome scenarios. 

​Support knowledge creation and further research through development of population-level models and analytical frameworks relevant to cancer early detection and policy.​ 

Informed by Patient and Public Involvement and Engagement (PPIE) discussion, findings will be interpreted and communicated with particular attention to fairness, acceptability, and the potential differential impact of screening or diagnostic strategies across population groups. This will include discussion of how alternative screening eligibility rules and diagnostic timelines may be understood by affected communities, and how findings should be communicated to avoid misinterpretation or unintended stigma. These perspectives will also help inform discussions with clinical, policy, and screening stakeholders about the practical implications of the findings for equitable screening and early diagnosis.
states.objective:
​​​​The Data will be used for the purpose of  ​​a research project: Population-level analysis of cancer natural history, diagnostic pathways and outcomes across cancer types and ethnic groups in England  

​​The research project aims to examine cancer incidence, diagnostic pathways, delays and outcomes across population groups, and to develop models (including breast cancer screening models) to assess impacts on mortality, inequalities and health service outcomes.  

​​The following are the aims/objectives of the processing:  

Workstream 1: Diagnostic delay across the 12 most common cancers

•	To understand cancer progression rates and quantify how diagnostic delay affects stage at diagnosis, mortality, and economic outcomes across the 12 most common cancers in England. 

•	To identify cancer types and population groups where timely diagnosis has the greatest impact. 

•	​To develop cancer-type-specific multistate models using national cancer registry data. 

Workstream 2: Breast cancer natural history and screening evaluation

•	​To develop ethnicity-specific models of breast cancer natural history and evaluate alternative screening strategies.

​The Data will be used to answer the following questions: 

​1) How does diagnostic delay influence the likelihood of being diagnosed with advanced-stage cancer and subsequent mortality across different cancer types? 

2) ​How do cancer progression, outcomes, and the impact of delay vary by ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and other patient characteristics? 

3) ​What are the health and economic impacts of different diagnostic timelines, and could cancer-specific timelines improve outcomes compared to the current uniform approach? 

4) ​What are the health and economic impacts of different diagnostic timelines, and could cancer-specific timelines improve outcomes compared to the current uniform approach? 

5) ​For breast cancer, how does natural history and progression differ across ethnic groups, and how might alternative screening strategies affect detection, outcomes, and inequalities?​
states.title: Population-level analysis of cancer natural history, diagnostic pathways and outcomes across cancer types and ethnic groups in England
